extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and legal practitioners handling infringement actions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting a declaration and for defendants' pleadings and evidentiary notices in patent infringement actions under early U.S. statute law (Act of 1836 and antecedents). Covers required allegations, assignment/recording issues, available defenses, and notice requirements for special matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must show plaintiff's title with convenient certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration in an action for the infringement of a patent should show a title in the plaintiff, with convenient certainty, and set forth all matters which are of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these allegations, the plaintiff fails to show a legal right to seek judgment. (§262) The several parts of the declaration should be considered in the order they occur in pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment of original and first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should commence with a recital that the plaintiff was 'the original and first inventor' of the subject-matter complained of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This averment is necessary notwithstanding the letters-patent because the patentee status must appear affirmatively at trial; letters-patent are only prima facie evidence. (§263)

rubrics_metrics.name: Averment of novelty and non-use/onsale
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should aver that the subject-matter was 'new and useful,' 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery,' and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (§264) These matters are essential elements of the plaintiff's title and should be expressly alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averring citizenship advisable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally safer practice to aver the citizenship of the patentee in the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether necessary has not been definitively determined, but averring citizenship avoids potential demurrer issues and is the safer course. (§265)

rubrics_metrics.name: Aver that letters-patent were duly obtained in due form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary to aver that the plaintiff, being the original and first inventor, obtained letters-patent for his invention in due form of law, under the seal of the patent office, signed and countersigned as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formerly patents bore presidential attestation; now aver that the patent was granted in the form prescribed by law (e.g., 'did obtain' them). The court will presume preliminary steps were rightly done when the grant is averred. (§265)

rubrics_metrics.name: Set forth substance of the grant and profert of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should set forth the substance of the grant (that letters-patent secured to the plaintiff for the statutory term the full and exclusive right of practising the invention) and should describe it briefly as in the letters-patent, of which profert should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the declaration quotes the patent, the specification need not be set out; defendant may require the specification via prayer of oyer. (§266)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude declaration with value, breach, and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should conclude by averring the value of the patent right, the breach by the defendant, and the damages sustained by the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (§267) These allegations support claims for relief and damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee must plead both patentee's and assignee's title and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff sues as assignee, he must set forth both the patentee's title and his own, and should aver that the assignments were duly recorded in the patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission to state recording may be cured by verdict if the declaration otherwise permits proof of recording at trial; recording may be proven before or after the action is brought. (§268–269)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant may plead general issue and give statute/special matters with notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 15th section of the Act of 1836, the defendant may plead the general issue and give the statute and certain special matters in evidence, provided written notice of such matters is given to plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The special matters include allegations that the specification does not contain the whole truth, that it contains more than necessary, that the patentee was not the original inventor of the thing patented (or a substantial part), prior public description/use/sale before application, or surreptitious/unjust obtaining by another. (§270)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice substitutes for a special plea and protects against surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the statutory notice is to allow defendants to rely on special matters under the general issue while protecting the plaintiff from surprise. The notice functions as a substitute for a special plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may nevertheless plead specially (in which case the plea itself is the notice) or plead general issue and give notice of special matter. The notice must be sufficiently specific. (§271)

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must specify names/residences and places for prior-use defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on prior invention, knowledge, or use, the defendant must state in his notice the names and places of residence of those he intends to prove had prior knowledge and where the thing had been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was added because prior construction suggested places need not be given; courts require specificity (e.g., cannot give notice of prior use 'in the United States' and then offer evidence of prior use in England). No witness may be examined for prior use without notice of name and residence. (§272)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses available under general issue without notice: non-infringement and license
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the general issue and without notice, the defendant may show that he never did the act complained of (i.e., did not infringe), or that he was acting under a license or purchase from the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (§274) These are basic factual defenses to infringement that do not require the statutory notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses available without notice: status of plaintiff/title/issuance defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Without notice the defendant may show that the plaintiff is an alien not entitled to a patent, that the plaintiff lacks good title as assignee, or that the patent was not duly issued according to law (e.g., deficiencies in signatures or public seal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (§274) These relate to the plaintiff's entitlement, title, and formal validity of the patent grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter non-patentability (not art/machine/manufacture/composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting novelty, the defendant may show that the invention is not a patentable subject — i.e., is not an 'art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' in the statutory sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct issue from lack of novelty (which falls under the statute and requires notice). It may be raised under the general issue without notice. (§275)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of utility (worthless or frivolous invention) as a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show, under the general issue and without notice, that the invention, though new, fails in point of utility and is worthless or frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of utility is a clear bar to the action both under the statute and general principles of law. (§276)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable the invention; ambiguity can void the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that there is no specification, or that the specification is so ambiguous and unintelligible that the court cannot determine what the invention is; if the specification does not describe the invention in clear and exact terms to distinguish it from others, the patent is void for ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is different from the statutory issue of concealment or addition made to deceive; a clear and distinct specification is essential to validity and may be put in issue by plea of not guilty without notice. (§277)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory special defense: concealment or addition to specification made to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: One statutory special defense is that the description and specification filed by the plaintiff 'does not contain the whole truth relative to his invention or discovery, or that it contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect; which concealment or addition shall fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense falls within the statutory list requiring written notice when the general issue is pleaded. Courts have struggled to define scope and distinguish it from mere ambiguity or insufficiency. (§279–280)

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict construction of notice and geographic limits of prior-use proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of special matter must be strictly construed; if the defendant's notice asserts prior use in a particular jurisdiction (e.g., the United States), he cannot be allowed to prove prior use elsewhere (e.g., England).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits the scope of evidence the defendant may introduce under the statutory notice. (§272)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between defective/ambiguous specification and intentional concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a doctrinal distinction: some decisions require that to render a patent void under the statute the defect or concealment must appear to have been made with intent to deceive the public; whereas at common law a specification so defective as to prevent a skilled person from making the invention could avoid the patent irrespective of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases and commentary debate whether the statute altered common-law rules; courts have sometimes held intent to deceive necessary to avoid the patent under the statute, while recognizing that wholly impracticable specifications may defraud the public regardless of intent. (§280–281; Whittemore v. Cutter and subsequent cases)
